questions.q: Why doesn't a free-tier RPC dev key reveal what matters for production usage?
options: A free tier hides compute-unit limits, the real uptime SLA, and geographic latency that only show up under sustained production load
Free tiers and production tiers are always functionally identical
Free-tier keys cannot be used for any testing purposes at all
Production load is always lower than free-tier limits allow
questions.explain: Rate limits, contractual SLAs, and edge-node latency only become visible and relevant once traffic resembles real production usage.

questions.q: When is an archive node required instead of a full node?
options: For fork testing at a specific historical block (Chapter 1, Lesson 4) or backfilling an indexer against old events
An archive node is never actually needed for any blockchain task
Only when sending brand-new transactions, never for reads
Full nodes and archive nodes provide identical data in all cases
questions.explain: A full node only holds recent state; historical state back to genesis requires an archive node, which fork testing and event backfilling both depend on.

questions.q: What problem does configuring a fallback provider (primary + backup) actually solve?
options: It prevents a single RPC provider's outage or rate-limiting from becoming the dApp's own outage
It doubles the compute units available from a single provider
It eliminates the need for any RPC provider at all
It converts a full node into an archive node automatically
questions.explain: A fallback configuration automatically switches to a backup provider if the primary is slow, rate-limited, or down, adding redundancy a single-provider setup lacks.

questions.q: What does choosing to self-host an RPC node actually trade away?
options: A monthly provider bill, in exchange for taking on patching, monitoring, and 24/7 uptime as your own team's responsibility
Nothing -- self-hosting is strictly free and has no operational cost
Access to any historical chain data whatsoever
The ability to ever use a managed provider again
questions.explain: Self-hosting removes third-party rate limits and fees but makes uptime, patching, and monitoring the team's own ongoing operational job.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what question does Chapter 5 take up next?
options: How do you actually know when something in the hosted off-chain stack, or the contracts it talks to, goes wrong?
How do you write a smart contract's first unit test?
How do you pick a Solidity compiler version?
How do you verify a contract on a block explorer?
questions.explain: Chapter 4 closes with the stack hosted and configured; Chapter 5, Monitoring & Incident Response, covers detecting when something goes wrong.
